title: Cauchy's Theorem: the Prime-Divisor Converse to Lagrange
content: Cauchy (1845) is the theorem that a prime p dividing |G| forces an element of order exactly p. Mathlib proves it via a fixed-point argument on the set of p-tuples with product 1 (exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card'); here we simply repackage it in Nat.card form and take primality as an ordinary hypothesis, installing the required `Fact p.Prime` instance internally so the theorem is directly applicable.
mathContext: $p \mid |G|,\ p$ prime $\Rightarrow \exists x \in G,\ \mathrm{ord}(x) = p$. This is the sharp prime-divisor slice of the converse to Lagrange.

title: Every Prime Divisor Yields a Cyclic Subgroup of That Order
content: An element x of order p generates the cyclic subgroup zpowers x, whose order is exactly orderOf x = p (Nat.card_zpowers). Because a group of prime order is cyclic (isCyclic_of_prime_card), that subgroup is cyclic. So the converse to Lagrange holds at the subgroup level for prime divisors — a statement that is false for composite divisors, as A₄ (order 12, no subgroup of order 6) shows.
mathContext: $\langle x\rangle = \mathrm{zpowers}(x)$ has $|\langle x\rangle| = \mathrm{ord}(x) = p$, and $|H| = p$ prime $\Rightarrow H$ cyclic.

title: |G| and exp(G) Have the Same Prime Factors
content: Cauchy gives the forward half of a clean equivalence: p | |G| ⟹ (Cauchy) an element of order p ⟹ p | exp(G) since every element order divides the exponent (order_dvd_exponent). The reverse half is elementary — exp(G) | |G| (Group.exponent_dvd_nat_card). The resulting iff, applied factorwise through Nat.mem_primeFactors, shows primeFactors(|G|) = primeFactors(exp(G)): the exponent can be far smaller than the order but loses no prime.
mathContext: $p \mid |G| \iff p \mid \exp(G)$, hence $\mathrm{primeFactors}(|G|) = \mathrm{primeFactors}(\exp(G))$, using $|G| \neq 0$ and $\exp(G) \neq 0$ for finite $G$.

title: Even Order ⟺ Contains an Involution (the p = 2 Case)
content: The classical fact that a finite group of even order contains an involution is just Cauchy at p = 2. The converse — an involution forces even order — is pure Lagrange: an order-2 element has order dividing |G|, so 2 | |G|. Packaging both directions gives the iff Even(|G|) ⟺ ∃ x, orderOf x = 2, and exists_involution_of_even_card restates the involution concretely as x ≠ 1 with x·x = 1.
mathContext: $2 \mid |G| \iff \exists x,\ x^2 = 1 \wedge x \neq 1$. Forward: Cauchy at $p=2$. Reverse: $\mathrm{ord}(x)=2 \mid |G|$.

title: Cauchy in S₃: a 3-Cycle and a Transposition
content: The symmetric group S₃ = Perm (Fin 3) has order 3! = 6 (Nat.card_perm). Since 2 and 3 both divide 6, Cauchy guarantees an element of order 2 (a transposition, via the involution corollary) and an element of order 3 (a 3-cycle, via cauchy directly). This concretely exhibits the abstract existence statements.
mathContext: $|S_3| = 3! = 6 = 2 \cdot 3$, so Cauchy yields elements of orders $2$ and $3$.
